fixes.explanation: Yes, friend, he says he's reciting his verses to the king. His heart is stirred by a noble theme, and he says his tongue is "…the pen of a skillful writer." (Psalm 45:1) A tongue that works like a pen. Mine works more like a smudge, and I'm the one holding the stamp.

Nope, no priests in this verse. The writer says, "…I recite my verses to the king…" (Psalm 45:1) The heading says the song is for the choirmaster, but the verse names the king as the one the verses are for.
Close, but the elders don't show up in this verse. The writer says he recites his verses "…to the king…" (Psalm 45:1) The verse names the king. So when you hear this psalm, think king.
Yes! The writer says, "Strap your sword at your side, O mighty warrior…" (Psalm 45:3) A sword at his side and a title like that. That's a warrior, baker.

I see why you'd pick judge, since justice comes up in this psalm. Still, verse 3 says, "Strap your sword at your side, O mighty warrior…" (Psalm 45:3) The word the writer uses is warrior. Judge is a fair guess, but it isn't the title in this verse.
Whoa, friend, afraid isn't the word. The writer says, "from palaces of ivory the harps make you glad." (Psalm 45:8) The harps make the king glad. Keep your eyes on that one little word.
That's right, friend. The writer says, "the queen stands at your right hand, adorned with the gold of Ophir." (Psalm 45:9) She's at his right hand, dressed in gold. Gold of Ophir, no less.

You got it, baker. The writer says, "Forget your people and your father's house, and the king will desire your beauty…" (Psalm 45:10-11) Notice who's doing the desiring: the king. That's a lot of attention for one song. I'd be blushing under this mustache.
Not this time. The writer says, "…and the king will desire your beauty…" (Psalm 45:11) The verse says desire. Sending her back home isn't in the song.

Whoa, friend, that's a sad ending, and it's not in the text. The writer says, "…and the king will desire your beauty…" (Psalm 45:11) The verse says the king will desire her beauty. Forgetting her name doesn't come up.
Yes, favor! The writer says, "men of wealth will seek your favor." (Psalm 45:12) Men of wealth seeking her favor. I just hope somebody likes my cookies enough to ask for another.
Yikes, that's a sharp turn. The verse is kinder: "men of wealth will seek your favor." (Psalm 45:12) The wealthy men seek her favor, which is a good thing to seek. Harm isn't in the verse.
Good guess, friend. But the verse says, "In colorful garments she is led to the king…" (Psalm 45:14) She's headed to the king. The temple doesn't come up in this part.

Not quite, baker. The text says, "They are led in with joy and gladness; they enter the palace of the king." (Psalm 45:15) Joy and gladness is how they're led in. Fear and trembling isn't in the verse.

Yes, friend! The writer says, "Your sons will succeed your fathers; you will make them princes throughout the land." (Psalm 45:16) Princes throughout the land, no less. That's a lot of royal titles to hand out.

Obey is a fair guess for a king's song. But the last verse says, "therefore the nations will praise you forever and ever." (Psalm 45:17) The writer says he will commemorate the name through all generations, and the nations praise because of it. I'd settle for one person praising a single batch of mine.
